103666.e: Around 22 or 23 September day and night are the same length again. Then astronomical autumn begins where we live.

103667.q: Which season is it in Australia when it is summer where we live?
103667.e: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere. There the seasons are exactly the other way round from ours.
103667.m: When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia.

103668.q: Which seasons do many countries near the equator have instead of summer and winter?
103668.e: At the equator the Sun is high all year round, so it is always warm. Instead of summer and winter, a rainy season and a dry season often take turns there.
103668.m: At the equator there is often a rainy season and a dry season instead of summer and winter.

103669.q: How many days does a leap year have?
103669.e: The Earth needs a little more than 365 days to go once round the Sun. That is why there is a 29 February almost every 4 years.

103670.q: Is the Earth closest to the Sun in summer?
a: No, it is closest at the beginning of January
103670.e: The Earth's orbit is almost a circle. The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, in the middle of our winter.
103670.m: The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January.

103671.q: Which large space telescope was launched into space on 25 December 2021?
103671.e: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched at Christmas 2021. It observes very distant galaxies with infrared light.
103671.m: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021.

103672.q: Which famous space telescope has been circling the Earth since 1990?
103672.e: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990. It has taken many famous pictures of stars and galaxies.
103672.m: The Hubble telescope has been circling the Earth since 1990.

103673.q: Why are large telescopes often built on high mountains?
a: Air and clouds get in the way less there
103673.e: On high mountains there is less air above the telescope. You are also often above the clouds and far away from city lights.
103673.m: On high mountains air and clouds get in the telescope's way less.

103674.q: What does a telescope collect so that you can see distant stars?
103674.e: With a lens or a mirror, a telescope collects much more light than the eye. That way you can see very faint stars too.

103675.q: What does a reflecting telescope use instead of a large lens?
103675.e: A reflecting telescope collects the light with a curved mirror. Even the biggest telescopes in the world are reflecting telescopes.
103675.m: A reflecting telescope collects light with a curved mirror.

103676.q: Why must you never look at the Sun through a telescope?
103676.e: A telescope concentrates the sunlight very strongly. That can destroy your eye in an instant.
103676.m: Never look at the Sun through a telescope.

103677.q: What is the well-known public observatory in the middle of Zurich called?
103677.e: The Urania Observatory has stood in the middle of Zurich since 1907. There you can look at the sky through a large telescope.
103677.m: The Urania Observatory is in Zurich.

103678.q: What is the part of a telescope you look into called?
103678.e: The eyepiece is at the end where your eye goes. You look at the image through this small piece of lens.
103678.m: You look into a telescope through the eyepiece.

103679.q: What is the main job of the cell wall of a plant cell?
103679.e: The cell wall is a sturdy covering around the cell. It supports the cell and gives it a firm shape.
103679.m: The cell wall makes the plant cell sturdy.

103680.q: What does the cell wall prevent when a plant cell takes in a lot of water?
103680.e: When the cell takes in water, its contents push outwards. The firm cell wall pushes back, so the plant cell doesn't burst.
103680.m: The cell wall protects the plant cell from bursting.

103682.q: Which substance from plant cell walls is used as a gelling agent when making jam?
103682.e: Pectin is a component of cell walls and is found in especially large amounts in apples and citrus fruits. It makes jam set; gelatine, on the other hand, comes from animals.
103682.m: Pectin from plant cell walls makes jam set.

103683.q: Which living things have cell walls made of chitin instead of cellulose?
103683.e: Fungi are not plants. Their cell walls are made of chitin, the same substance that is found in the shells of insects.
103683.m: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin.

103684.q: Do animal cells have a cell wall?
103684.e: Animal cells are surrounded only by a thin, flexible cell membrane. They have no firm cell wall.
103684.m: Animal cells have no cell wall.

103685.q: Does the cell wall let water and dissolved substances through?
103685.e: The cell wall is like a coarse net of fibres and lets water and small dissolved substances through easily. The real selection is only made by the cell membrane.
103685.m: The cell wall is highly permeable to water.

103686.q: In which plant material do the cells have especially thick, lignified cell walls?
a: In the wood of a tree trunk
In the petal of a rose
In the flesh of a tomato
103686.e: In wood, the cell walls are greatly thickened and lignified. That is why a tree trunk is so hard and strong.
103686.m: Wood is hard because its cell walls are thick and lignified.

103687.q: Which property best describes the cell membrane?
a: It only lets certain substances through
It lets no substances through at all
It lets all substances through equally
103687.e: The cell membrane is partially permeable (selectively permeable). It controls which substances get into and out of the cell.
103687.m: The cell membrane selects which substances get into the cell.

103688.q: Where is the cell membrane in a plant cell?
a: On the inside, close against the cell wall
On the outside of the cell wall
In the middle of the nucleus
103688.e: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and, in plant cells, lies close against the inside of the cell wall.
103688.m: In plants, the cell membrane lies against the inside of the cell wall.

103689.q: What is the cell membrane mainly made of?
a: A double layer of fatty substances
103689.e: The cell membrane is a very thin double layer of lipids, which are fatty substances. It surrounds the whole cell.
103689.m: The cell membrane is a double layer of fatty substances with proteins built in.

103690.q: What is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane called?
103690.e: In osmosis, water moves through a partially permeable membrane towards the side with the higher concentration of dissolved substances.
103690.m: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

103691.q: What happens to a lettuce leaf that lies in strong salt water for a long time?
a: It goes limp because it loses water
103691.e: The salt draws water out of the cells. The cells shrink and the leaf goes soft and limp.
103691.m: Salt water draws water out of plant cells.

103692.q: Which cell part do plant cells, animal cells and bacteria have in common?
103692.e: Every living cell is surrounded by a cell membrane. A cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, on the other hand, are only found in plants.
103692.m: All living cells have a cell membrane.

103693.q: Roughly how thick is a cell membrane?
a: About a tenth of a millimetre
103693.e: A cell membrane is only a few millionths of a millimetre, that is a few nanometres, thick. That is why it can't be resolved on its own with a light microscope.
103693.m: The cell membrane is only a few nanometres thin.

103694.q: Which building blocks in the cell membrane act as channels and pumps for substances?
103694.e: Proteins are built into the fatty double layer of the membrane. Some form channels, others pump substances through the membrane in a targeted way.
103694.m: Proteins in the cell membrane act as channels and pumps.

103695.e: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll. It captures light for photosynthesis.
103695.m: Chlorophyll is the green pigment of chloroplasts.

103696.q: What takes place in the chloroplasts?
103696.e: In the chloroplasts, plants use light to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen. This is photosynthesis.
103696.m: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.

103697.q: Which energy do chloroplasts use for their work?
103697.e: Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy. That is why green plants need light to grow.
103697.m: Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy.

103698.q: Where are the chloroplasts in a plant cell?
103698.e: The chloroplasts float in the cytoplasm. They are often near the edge of the cell, where they get a lot of light.
103698.m: Chloroplasts are in the cytoplasm of the plant cell.

103699.q: In which cells of a leaf are there especially many chloroplasts?
103699.e: The palisade cells lie directly under the upper surface of the leaf and are packed with chloroplasts. Most photosynthesis takes place there.
103699.m: The palisade cells are the leaf's main power station.

103700.q: Which parts of a plant normally have no chloroplasts?
103700.e: Roots grow in the dark soil and don't carry out photosynthesis. That is why they normally have no chloroplasts.
103700.m: Roots in the soil usually have no chloroplasts.

103702.q: What shape are chloroplasts in land plants usually?
103702.e: In land plants, chloroplasts are usually lens-shaped and only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. In some algae, however, there are also ribbon-shaped or star-shaped chloroplasts.
103702.m: The chloroplasts of land plants look like little lenses.

103703.q: What happens to the green pigment when a tomato ripens?
a: It is broken down and red pigments form
It gets darker and darker green
103703.e: As it ripens, the tomato breaks down the chlorophyll and forms red pigments. That is why it turns from green to red.
103703.m: Ripe tomatoes break down the green and turn red.

103704.q: What is the job of the large vacuole in a plant cell?
a: It stores water and dissolved substances
It forms the firm cell wall
103704.e: The vacuole is a store full of cell sap. This consists mainly of water with dissolved salts, sugars and pigments.
103704.m: The vacuole is the water store of the plant cell.

103705.q: What is the liquid in the vacuole called?
103705.e: The vacuole is filled with cell sap. This consists mainly of water with dissolved salts, sugars, pigments and other substances.
103705.m: The vacuole is filled with cell sap.

103706.q: What is the pressure called with which the full vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall?
103706.e: The internal pressure of a plant cell that is full to bursting is called turgor. It keeps non-woody plant parts such as leaves firm.
103706.m: Turgor keeps leaves and young stems firm.

103707.q: Why does a plant wilt if it gets too little water?
103707.e: Without water the vacuoles shrink and the pressure in the cells drops. The leaves lose their tension and hang down limply.
103707.m: A plant wilts when its vacuoles lose water.

103708.q: What happens to purple red cabbage juice when you add vinegar?
103708.e: The pigments in the cell sap of red cabbage are called anthocyanins. They change colour depending on acidity: with vinegar the juice turns red, with soap rather green.
103708.m: The colour of red cabbage juice shows whether something is acidic.

103709.q: How much of the cell volume can the central vacuole take up in a fully grown plant cell?
103709.e: In fully grown plant cells, the central vacuole often fills most of the cell, up to about 90 per cent of the volume.
103709.m: The central vacuole can fill almost the whole plant cell.

103710.q: How do the vacuoles change as a young plant cell grows?
a: Small vacuoles merge into one large one
The vacuoles move into the nucleus
103710.e: Young plant cells have many small vacuoles. As they grow, they take in water and merge into one large central vacuole.
103710.m: As the cell grows, many small vacuoles become one large one.

103711.q: Which substances do many plants store in the vacuole to protect themselves from animals that eat them?
103711.e: Bitter and poisonous substances are often stored in the vacuole. This puts off animals that feed on the plant.
103711.m: Many plants hide poisons in their vacuoles.

103712.e: The genetic information is in the nucleus in the form of DNA. It contains the blueprints for all the proteins of the cell.
103712.m: The nucleus holds the cell's genetic information.

103713.q: What is the double covering around the nucleus called?
103713.e: The nucleus is surrounded by a nuclear envelope made of two membranes. It separates the genetic material from the rest of the cell contents.
103713.m: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes.

103714.q: Through which openings do substances get into and out of the nucleus?
103714.e: The nuclear envelope is pierced by many nuclear pores. Substances and messenger molecules pass through them between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
103714.m: Nuclear pores are the gates of the nucleus.

103715.q: Which instrument can you use to see the nucleus of a cell?
103715.e: Cells are far too small for the naked eye. Under the microscope you see the nucleus as a round structure, especially when it is stained.
103715.m: You can only see nuclei under the microscope.

103716.q: What is the dense body in the nucleus where building blocks for ribosomes are made called?
103716.e: In the nucleus you can often see a dark body, the nucleolus. Components of the ribosomes are made there.
103716.m: Building blocks of ribosomes are made in the nucleolus.

103717.q: How many nuclei does an ordinary living plant cell have?
103717.e: A normal plant cell has exactly one nucleus. As the control centre, it directs the processes in the cell.
103717.m: A normal plant cell has a single nucleus.

103718.q: Which cells in human blood have no nucleus?
103718.e: Red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature. That gives them more room to carry oxygen.
103718.m: Red blood cells have no nucleus.

103719.q: What are the structures called into which the genetic material condenses before a cell divides?
103719.e: Before division, the long DNA is wound up tightly. This forms chromosomes, which can be seen under the microscope.
103719.m: Before division, the genetic material condenses into chromosomes.

a: The cell contents inside the cell membrane, apart from the nucleus
The outer layer of the cell wall
The genetic material in the nucleus
103720.e: The cytoplasm is everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus. The organelles are found in it.
103720.m: The organelles of the cell are in the cytoplasm.

103721.q: What is cytoplasm mostly made of?
103721.e: Cytoplasm consists mostly of water. Proteins, salts, sugars and many other substances are dissolved in it.

103722.q: What is the movement of the cell contents that you can observe in the small leaves of Canadian waterweed called?
103722.e: In the cells of Canadian waterweed, the cytoplasm constantly flows round in a circle. This cytoplasmic streaming distributes substances in the cell.
103722.m: Cytoplasmic streaming distributes substances in the cell.

103723.q: What is found in the cytoplasm of a cell?
103723.e: The organelles, for example mitochondria and chloroplasts, are found in the cytoplasm. The cell wall lies right on the outside of the plant cell.
103723.m: The organelles are in the cytoplasm.

103724.q: Which organelle in the cytoplasm supplies the cell with energy?
103724.e: In the mitochondria, sugar is broken down with oxygen. This releases the energy that the cell needs.
103724.m: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell.

103725.q: What gives a plant cell firm support and shape from the outside?
103725.e: The cellulose cell wall surrounds the plant cell like a firm casing. Animal cells have no cell wall.
103725.m: The cell wall gives the plant cell support.

103726.q: Which organelle in the cytoplasm of a plant cell carries out photosynthesis?
103726.e: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll. With it, the plant makes sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.
103726.m: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.

103727.q: Where is the cytoplasm in a fully grown plant cell usually found?
a: As a thin layer at the edge
As a ball in the middle
103727.e: The large central vacuole pushes the cytoplasm to the edge. There it forms a thin layer between the vacuole and the cell wall.
103727.m: In old plant cells, the cytoplasm is a thin coating at the edge.

103728.q: What is the job of mitochondria?
a: They release energy through cellular respiration
103728.e: In the mitochondria, nutrients such as glucose are broken down. The cell can use the energy released for its work.

103729.e: Plant cells also need energy for their life processes. That is why they have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
103729.m: Plant cells have chloroplasts and mitochondria.

103730.q: Which gas do mitochondria use up during cellular respiration?
103730.e: In cellular respiration, glucose is broken down with oxygen. Without oxygen this process doesn't work.
103730.m: Mitochondria need oxygen for cellular respiration.

103732.q: Why do muscle cells have especially many mitochondria?
a: They need a lot of energy
They store a lot of water
103732.e: Muscles work hard and constantly need energy for it. The mitochondria supply it, which is why muscle cells have especially many of them.
103732.m: Cells that need a lot of energy have many mitochondria.

103733.q: How many membranes surround a mitochondrion?
103733.e: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. So it is surrounded by two membranes.

103734.q: Which nickname is often used for mitochondria?
103734.e: Because mitochondria provide most of the usable energy, they are often called the power stations of the cell.
103734.m: Mitochondria are called the power stations of the cell.

103735.q: Which substances are produced as waste during cellular respiration in the mitochondria?
103735.e: When sugar is broken down with oxygen, carbon dioxide and water are produced. The carbon dioxide is given off.
103735.m: Cellular respiration produces carbon dioxide and water.

103736.q: An eyepiece magnifies 10 times and the objective lens 40 times. What is the total magnification?
103736.e: You multiply the magnifications of the eyepiece and the objective: 10 × 40 = 400. So the image is magnified 400 times.
103736.m: Total magnification is eyepiece magnification times objective magnification.

103737.q: You move the slide to the left under the microscope. Which way does the image move?
103737.e: A light microscope shows the image upside down and reversed left to right. That is why the image always moves in the opposite direction to the slide.
103737.m: In a microscope the image is upside down and reversed.

103738.q: What is the lens on a microscope that you look into with your eye called?
103738.e: The eyepiece sits at the top of the tube, right at your eye. It is also called the ocular, from the Latin word “oculus” for eye.
103738.m: You look into the microscope through the eyepiece.

103739.q: What is the lens on a microscope that sits just above the specimen called?
103739.e: The objective lens faces the object, that is the specimen. It produces the first magnified image.
103739.m: The objective lens sits just above the specimen.

103740.q: Which part of the microscope do you use to control the amount of light?
103740.e: The diaphragm under the stage lets more or less light through. This is how brightness and contrast are adjusted.
103740.m: You control brightness and contrast with the diaphragm.

103741.q: Which knob do you use first to bring the microscope image roughly into focus?
103741.e: You first use the large coarse focus knob to find a roughly sharp image. Then you adjust it exactly with the fine focus knob.
103741.m: First focus with the coarse knob, then with the fine knob.

103742.q: Which magnification do you start with when using a microscope?
103742.e: With the lowest magnification you see the largest area and find the interesting spot more easily. After that you switch to stronger objectives.
103742.m: When using a microscope, always start with the lowest magnification.

103743.q: Up to what magnification are images from a good light microscope useful?
103743.e: Because of the wavelength of light, images magnified at most about 1,000 to 2,000 times are useful with a light microscope. For more you need an electron microscope.
103743.m: For greater magnification than a light microscope, you need an electron microscope.

103744.q: What is the rotating part that holds several objective lenses called?
103744.e: Objectives with different magnifications are mounted on the objective turret. By turning it you switch quickly between them.
103744.m: You change objectives on the objective turret.

103745.q: Which part of a kitchen onion do you use for an onion skin slide?
a: The thin skin on the inside of a scale
The green shoot in the middle
103745.e: On the inside of a fleshy onion scale there is a wafer-thin skin. It consists of only one layer of cells and is therefore transparent enough for the microscope.
103745.m: For the slide you use the thin inner skin of an onion scale.

103746.q: Why can't you see any chloroplasts in the cells of onion skin?
a: The onion scales grow without light
103746.e: The scales lie inside the onion in the dark and only store nutrients. They don't carry out photosynthesis and therefore have no chloroplasts.
103746.m: Onion skin cells have no chloroplasts because they grow in the dark.

103747.q: What do you put on the slide before laying the onion skin on it?
103747.e: The skin is spread out in a drop of water. That way it doesn't dry out and the cells stay in their natural state.
103747.m: A wet mount lies in a drop of water.

103748.q: How do you put the cover slip on so that no air bubbles form?
a: Lower it at an angle from the side
Let it drop flat onto it
103748.e: You place the cover slip at an angle at the edge of the drop and slowly lower it. This pushes the air out to the side.
103748.m: Lower a cover slip slowly and at an angle.

103749.q: Which stain can be used to colour the nuclei of onion skin cells blue?
103749.e: Methylene blue stains the nuclei in particular a strong blue. That makes them much easier to see under the microscope.
103749.m: Methylene blue makes nuclei easy to see.

103750.q: What do onion skin cells look like under the microscope?
103750.e: Onion skin cells are elongated and lie close together. The image is reminiscent of a brick wall.
103750.m: Onion skin cells lie side by side like bricks.

103751.q: Which tool do you use to peel off the fine onion skin?
103751.e: With the tweezers you grip the thin skin and carefully peel it off. A pipette, on the other hand, is used to drip liquids.
103751.m: The onion skin is peeled off with tweezers.

103752.q: What do you call a slide made from fresh material in a drop of water?
103752.e: A wet mount is made from living material and only lasts a short time. Permanent slides, on the other hand, are preserved and sealed.
103752.m: A wet mount shows living material and doesn't last long.

103753.q: What is the small glass plate you put the specimen on called?
103753.e: The slide is a rectangular glass plate that you put the specimen on. The thinner cover slip goes on top.
103753.m: The specimen lies on the slide.

103754.q: What is the nuclear division called in which two daughter nuclei with the same genetic information are formed?
103754.e: In mitosis, the genetic information is shared out equally between two daughter nuclei. Both daughter cells therefore receive the same genes.
103754.m: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter nuclei.

103755.q: What must be doubled in the cell before it divides?
103755.e: So that each daughter cell receives the complete genetic information, the DNA is copied exactly beforehand.
103755.m: The genetic material is doubled before every cell division.

103756.q: How many daughter cells are produced in an ordinary cell division?
103756.e: In cell division, one parent cell divides into two daughter cells. Both receive the same genetic information.
103756.m: In division, one cell becomes two.

103757.q: What do living things need cell division for?
a: To grow and to heal wounds
103757.e: Cell division produces new cells. That is how a living thing grows, and how damaged tissue is replaced.
103757.m: Living things grow through cell division.

103758.q: How does a plant cell form the new dividing wall between the daughter cells?
a: Through a cell plate in the middle
By pinching in from the outside
103758.e: In plant cells, a cell plate forms in the middle of the cell and grows outwards. Animal cells, on the other hand, pinch in from the outside.
103758.m: When plant cells divide, they form a new wall in the middle.

103759.q: Where do a plant's cells divide especially often?
a: In the tips of the root and shoot
103759.e: At the tips of roots and shoots there are growth tissues. The cells there divide all the time, and the plant grows longer.
103759.m: Plants grow at their tips through many cell divisions.

103760.q: What is the apparatus of fine fibres that pulls the chromosomes apart during mitosis called?
103760.e: The spindle apparatus consists of fine protein tubes. It attaches to the chromosomes and pulls their halves apart.
103760.m: The spindle apparatus shares the chromosomes out between the daughter cells.

103761.q: What happens to the nuclear envelope at the start of mitosis?
103761.e: At the start of mitosis the nuclear envelope breaks down so that the spindle apparatus can reach the chromosomes. At the end, a new envelope forms around each daughter nucleus.
103761.m: The nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis and forms again afterwards.

103762.q: Which solution is used in class to test for starch?
103762.e: Iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide), also called Lugol's solution, reacts with starch and clearly changes its colour. That makes it very easy to detect starch.
103762.m: You test for starch with iodine solution.

103764.q: How can you make starch grains from a potato visible?
a: Cut the potato and look at the juice under the microscope
Freeze the potato and shake it
Dry the potato in the sun
Touch the potato with a magnet
103764.e: If you scrape a little from a cut potato, you can see lots of small starch grains under the microscope. With iodine solution they turn blue-violet.
103764.m: You can see potato starch grains under the microscope.

103765.q: What can you see in potato starch grains under the microscope?
103765.e: Potato starch grains show fine layered rings around a point. They form because the starch is laid down in layers.
103765.m: Starch grains grow in layers like onion rings.

103766.q: Where does a leaf temporarily store starch during the day?
103766.e: When photosynthesis is strong, surplus sugar is stored temporarily as starch in the chloroplasts. At night it is broken down and carried away.
103766.m: Leaves store starch in the chloroplasts during the day.

103768.q: In which part of a grain of wheat are most of the starch grains found?
103768.e: The endosperm makes up most of the grain and is filled with starch grains. It serves as a food store for the embryo.
103768.m: The endosperm of a cereal grain is full of starch.

103769.q: Plasmodesmata are tiny channels in the cell wall. What do they connect?
103769.e: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell walls of plant cells. In this way the insides of neighbouring cells are connected to each other.
103769.m: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells through the cell wall.

103770.q: What are the fine channels between plant cells, the plasmodesmata, for?
103770.e: Water, sugar and messenger substances pass directly from cell to cell through plasmodesmata.
103770.m: Plasmodesmata allow exchange between plant cells.

103771.q: Why do plant cells need connecting channels like plasmodesmata?
a: Because their firm cell wall would otherwise separate them
103771.e: Plant cells are surrounded by a firm cell wall. Without plasmodesmata they would be cut off from one another.
103771.m: Plasmodesmata pass through the firm cell wall of plant cells.

103772.q: Do animal cells have plasmodesmata too?
a: No, they have no cell wall
103772.e: Plasmodesmata are found in plants, whose cells have a cell wall. Animal cells have no cell wall and are connected in other ways.
103772.m: Plasmodesmata are typical of plant cells.

103773.q: What can pass through the plasmodesmata from one plant cell to the next?
103773.e: The channels are tiny. Only dissolved substances such as water, sugar and messenger substances fit through.
103773.m: Water and sugar pass through plasmodesmata.

103774.q: Some plant viruses use the fine channels between plant cells. What for?
a: To move from cell to cell
103774.e: Many plant viruses widen the plasmodesmata and travel through the plant this way. As they do, the disease spreads.
103774.m: Plant viruses travel from cell to cell through the plasmodesmata.

a: In the cell wall between two plant cells
103775.e: Plasmodesmata cross the cell wall that separates two neighbouring cells. That way the cells stay connected.
103775.m: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell wall.

a: So tiny that you need a very powerful microscope
103776.e: Plasmodesmata are much smaller even than a cell. You can only see them with an electron microscope.
103776.m: You can only see plasmodesmata with a very powerful microscope.

103874.q: Which two large joints does the humerus form part of?
103874.e: At the top, the head of the humerus sits in the socket of the shoulder blade; at the bottom the bone forms the elbow joint with the ulna and radius.
103874.m: The humerus connects the shoulder with the elbow.

103875.q: Which two bones join the humerus at the elbow?
103875.e: There are two bones in the forearm, the ulna and the radius. Together with the humerus they form the elbow joint.
103875.m: The humerus, ulna and radius meet at the elbow.

103876.q: What kind of joint does the head of the humerus form with the shoulder blade?
103876.e: The round head of the humerus sits in a socket of the shoulder blade. That is why you can move your arm in almost every direction.
103876.m: The shoulder joint is a ball and socket joint.

103877.q: What is the round upper end of the humerus called?
103877.e: The upper end of the humerus is a half ball covered with cartilage. It glides in the joint surface of the shoulder blade.
103877.m: The head of the humerus is the round end of the bone.

103878.q: Which large shoulder muscle is attached to the side of the humerus and lifts the arm sideways?
103878.e: The deltoid covers the shoulder like a cap and is attached to a rough spot on the shaft of the humerus. It lifts the arm sideways.
103878.m: The deltoid forms the round shoulder and lifts the arm.

103879.q: Which part of the humerus breaks especially often in older people after a fall?
a: The upper end near the shoulder
The lower end at the elbow
The groove of the radial nerve
103879.e: A fracture near the head of the humerus is one of the most common fractures in older people. The bone is often weakened by bone loss.
103879.m: In old age the upper arm often breaks near the shoulder.

103880.q: Which part of the skeleton does the humerus belong to?
103880.e: Arms and hands together form the upper limb. The humerus is its top and longest bone.
103880.m: The humerus is the longest bone of the arm.

103881.q: What else can be injured when the humerus breaks?
a: A nerve that controls the hand
103881.e: An important nerve, the radial nerve, runs around the shaft of the humerus. If it is injured in the fracture, the hand can hang limp.
103881.m: When the upper arm breaks, a nerve can be injured.

103882.q: On which side of the forearm is the ulna?
a: In the middle of the back of the hand
103882.e: If you hold your palm facing forwards, the ulna lies on the inside, on the little finger side.
103882.m: The ulna is on the little finger side.

103883.q: Which part of the ulna forms the hard point of the elbow?
103883.e: The upper end of the ulna forms a strong projection, the olecranon. You feel it when you lean on your elbow.
103883.m: The point of the elbow belongs to the ulna.

103884.q: Which forearm bone is the stronger one near the elbow?
103884.e: The ulna is thick at the top near the elbow and carries the large olecranon there. Towards the wrist it gets narrower.
103884.m: At the elbow, the ulna is the thick bone.

103885.q: Which of the two forearm bones is longer in adults?
a: It differs from arm to arm
103885.e: The ulna reaches from the elbow to the wrist and sticks out above the radius at the top with the olecranon. That is why it is a little longer.
103885.m: The ulna is the longer forearm bone.

103886.q: What is the Latin technical term for this forearm bone on the little finger side?
103886.e: In technical language the bone is called the ulna. The name of the ulnar nerve, nervus ulnaris, comes from it, for example.
103886.m: The forearm bone on the little finger side is called the ulna.

103887.q: How many long bones make up the forearm?
103887.e: The forearm has two long bones: the ulna on the little finger side and the radius on the thumb side.
103887.m: The forearm is made up of the ulna and the radius.

103888.q: Which forearm bone is the humerus’s most important partner at the elbow?
103888.e: The ulna grips the pulley-shaped end of the humerus with a pincer-like notch. This is where the arm bends and straightens.
103888.m: At the elbow, the ulna forms a hinge with the upper arm.

103889.q: Which bump can you feel on the wrist on the little finger side?
103889.e: The lower end of the ulna is called the head of the ulna. It sticks out as a round bump on the back of the hand on the little finger side.
103889.m: The bump on the wrist on the little finger side is the end of the ulna.

103890.q: On which side of the forearm is the radius?
a: On the back of the elbow
In the middle of the palm
103890.e: The radius runs from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist. There it is wide and easy to feel.
103890.m: The radius is on the thumb side.

103891.q: Which fracture is one of the most common in humans?
a: A broken radius at the wrist
103891.e: When people fall, they often catch themselves with an outstretched hand. The radius often breaks just above the wrist, which is why this fracture is so common.
103891.m: When you fall on your hand, the radius often breaks.

103892.q: Which movement does the radius make possible by turning around the ulna?
a: Turning the hand palm up and palm down
Lifting the arm above the head
Closing the fingers into a fist
Tilting the head to the side
103892.e: When you turn your hand over, the radius rotates around the ulna and crosses it. That way the palm faces up one moment and down the next.
103892.m: The radius turns around the ulna and so turns the hand.

103893.q: Where on the wrist do you usually feel the pulse?
a: On the thumb side above the radius
On the little finger side above the ulna
On the back of the hand above the knuckles
In the middle of the fingertip
103893.e: On the thumb side an artery lies right above the radius. You press it lightly against the bone and feel the pulse.
103893.m: You feel the pulse on the thumb side of the wrist.

103894.q: Which two bones make up the forearm?
103894.e: Two bones lie side by side in the forearm: the radius on the thumb side and the ulna on the little finger side.
103894.m: The forearm is made up of the radius and the ulna.

103895.q: What shape is the upper end of the radius at the elbow?
a: A ring with a big hole
103895.e: The head of the radius is a small disc covered with cartilage. It turns inside a ring-shaped ligament when you turn your hand.
103895.m: The head of the radius turns at the elbow.

103896.q: Which forearm bone forms most of the wrist joint with the carpal bones?
103896.e: The radius is wide at its lower end and carries a joint surface for the carpal bones. The ulna only takes part there through a disc of cartilage.
103896.m: The wrist is formed mainly by the radius.

103897.q: Which muscle is attached to the radius and bends the arm at the elbow?
103897.e: The tendon of the two-headed upper arm muscle (biceps) is attached to a bump on the radius. When it contracts, the arm bends.
103897.m: The biceps pulls on the radius and bends the arm.

103898.q: Why does a knock to the shin hurt so much?
a: The bone lies right under the skin
The bone is hollow and empty inside
There is a big muscle there
103898.e: At the front of the shin, almost no muscle or fat protects the bone. The sensitive outer layer of the bone lies directly under the skin.
103898.m: The front of the shin has hardly any padding.

103899.q: Which bone in the lower leg carries most of the body’s weight?
103899.e: The strong tibia passes the weight from the knee to the ankle. The thin fibula carries only a little.
103899.m: The tibia is the weight-bearing bone of the lower leg.

103900.q: Which ankle bump belongs to the tibia?
103900.e: The lower end of the tibia forms the bony bump on the inside of the ankle. You can feel it clearly under the skin.
103900.m: The inner ankle is the end of the tibia.

103901.q: Which thin bone lies next to the tibia in the lower leg?
103901.e: The lower leg has two bones: the strong tibia and the thin fibula. The ulna and radius are in the forearm.
103901.m: The tibia and fibula make up the lower leg.

103902.q: Which bone does the tibia form the knee joint with?
103902.e: The flat top of the tibia, the tibial plateau, carries the rounded ends of the thighbone. The menisci lie in between.
103902.m: The thighbone and tibia meet in the knee.

103903.q: Where is the kneecap tendon attached to the tibia?
a: At the bump below the knee
In the middle of the fibula
103903.e: Below the knee you can feel a bony bump at the front. That is where the kneecap tendon ends, through which the thigh muscle straightens the leg.
103903.m: Below the knee, the kneecap tendon pulls on the tibia.

103904.q: Why do sporty teenagers sometimes have pain at the bump below the knee while they are growing?
a: The kneecap tendon pulls hard on the growing spot
The skin is too thin there
The knee has too little blood
103904.e: With lots of jumping and running, the kneecap tendon pulls hard on the growth zone of the tibia. That can hurt; it is called Osgood-Schlatter disease.
103904.m: Strong pulling on the growing tibia can cause pain in teenagers.

103905.q: Which protective equipment must football players wear under the rules to protect the shin?
103905.e: Under the rules of football, shin pads are compulsory equipment. They protect the barely padded bone from kicks.
103905.m: In football, shin pads protect against painful kicks.

103906.q: Where is the fibula in the lower leg?
a: On the outside next to the tibia
On the inside next to the tibia
103906.e: The fibula is the thin bone on the outside of the lower leg. It runs parallel to the thicker tibia.
103906.m: The fibula is the slim bone on the outside of the lower leg.

103907.q: Which bone lies next to the fibula in the lower leg?
103907.e: The lower leg has two bones: the thick tibia on the inside and the thin fibula on the outside. The ulna and radius are in the forearm.
103907.m: The lower leg contains the tibia and the fibula.

103908.q: Which of the two lower leg bones is thinner?
103908.e: The fibula is slim and carries only a little weight. The thick tibia carries most of the load.
103908.m: The fibula is the thinner lower leg bone.

103909.q: Is the fibula directly part of the knee joint?
a: No, it lies below the knee
No, it ends at the thigh
103909.e: The head of the fibula is joined to the tibia at the side below the knee. It does not take part in the knee joint itself.
103909.m: The fibula does not reach into the knee joint.

103910.q: Which bony bump does the lower end of the fibula form?
103910.e: You can feel the lower end of the fibula on the outside of the ankle as the outer ankle. The inner ankle is formed by the tibia.
103910.m: The fibula ends at the bottom in the outer ankle.

103911.q: Why can a piece of the fibula be taken to replace bone elsewhere?
a: It carries only a little body weight
103911.e: Because the fibula carries hardly any load, part of it can be removed without making walking difficult. Surgeons use it, for example, to rebuild a jawbone.
103911.m: The fibula carries little weight and can therefore serve as a replacement bone.

103912.q: What is the fibula important for, despite carrying little weight?
a: The stability of the ankle joint
103912.e: With the outer ankle, the fibula and the tibia grip the ankle bone like a fork. That keeps the upper ankle joint stable at the sides.
103912.m: The fibula stabilises the ankle from the outside.

103913.q: What is mainly attached to the thin fibula?
a: Many muscles of the lower leg
The ribs of the rib cage
103913.e: The fibula serves as an attachment for many muscles, such as the fibular muscles on the outside. These lift the outer edge of the foot.
103913.m: Many lower leg muscles are attached to the fibula.

a: At the top of the back of the rib cage
At the front of the chest
At the side of the neck
103914.e: The shoulder blade lies on the upper part of the back of the rib cage. It reaches roughly from the second to the seventh rib.
103914.m: The shoulder blade covers the upper ribs at the back.

103915.q: Roughly what shape is the shoulder blade?
a: Long and round like a tube
103915.e: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone. Its technical name is scapula.
103915.m: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone.

103916.q: Which bone is the shoulder blade joined to by a small joint at the top of the shoulder?
103916.e: At the top of the shoulder, the shoulder blade and collarbone meet in the acromioclavicular joint. In this way the collarbone connects the arm to the trunk.
103916.m: The collarbone connects the shoulder blade to the breastbone.

103917.q: How is the shoulder blade mainly attached to the trunk?
a: By a ball and socket joint on the ribs
By a joint on the spine
103917.e: The shoulder blade has no real bony joint with the ribs or spine. Many muscles hold it in place and let it glide over the rib cage.
103917.m: Muscles hold the shoulder blade in place on the back.

103918.q: What is the spine of the scapula?
a: A bony ridge on the back of the shoulder blade
A tendon on the upper arm
A piece of cartilage in the breastbone
103918.e: The spine of the scapula is a strong bony ridge that runs across the back of the shoulder blade. It ends on the outside at the top of the shoulder.
103918.m: A bony ridge you can feel runs across the shoulder blade.

103919.q: What do the muscles that run from the shoulder blade to the head of the humerus do?
a: They hold the head of the humerus in its socket
103919.e: Four muscles surround the head of the humerus like a cuff. They turn the arm and hold the shoulder joint together. They are called the rotator cuff.
103919.m: Muscles from the shoulder blade hold the shoulder joint together.

103920.q: Which bone forms the shoulder joint together with the upper arm?
103920.e: The head of the humerus sits in the socket of the shoulder blade. Together they form the shoulder joint.
103920.m: The shoulder joint lies between the shoulder blade and the upper arm.

103921.q: What is it called when the shoulder blade sticks out clearly from the back?
103921.e: If a muscle that presses the shoulder blade against the ribs is weakened, its inner edge sticks out like a wing. This is called a winged scapula.
103921.m: A weak muscle can make the shoulder blade stick out.

103922.q: How many bones fuse to form each hip bone during the teenage years?
103922.e: The hip bone is formed from the ilium, ischium and pubis. These three parts grow together in the hip socket during the teenage years.
103922.m: Each hip bone is made of three fused bones.

103923.q: Which part of the skeleton do the two hip bones belong to?
103923.e: Together with the sacrum, the two hip bones form the pelvis. It connects the spine with the legs.
103923.m: The hip bones belong to the pelvis.

103924.q: Which bones together form the pelvic ring?
a: Two hip bones and the sacrum
Two shoulder blades and the breastbone
103924.e: The two hip bones are joined to each other at the front and to the sacrum at the back. That makes a stable ring of bone.
103924.m: The pelvis is a ring of two hip bones and the sacrum.

103925.q: Which upper edge of the hip bone can you feel at the side of your waist?
103925.e: The iliac crest is the upper, curved edge of the ilium. You feel it when you put your hands on your hips.
103925.m: You feel the iliac crest when you put your hands on your hips.

103926.q: Where do doctors often take bone marrow for a test?
103926.e: The iliac crest is easy to reach under the skin and contains a lot of red bone marrow. That is why marrow is often taken from there.
103926.m: Bone marrow is often taken from the iliac crest.

103927.q: Which part of the hip bone do you sit on?
103927.e: The sitting bones are two strong bony bumps at the bottom of the pelvis. You can feel them clearly on a hard chair.
103927.m: When you sit, the sitting bones carry your weight.

103928.q: What job does the pelvis do in the skeleton?
a: It passes the weight of the trunk to the legs
It protects the brain from knocks
It moves the fingers of the hand
103928.e: The pelvis passes the load of the trunk to the hip joints and so to the legs. It also supports the abdominal organs from below.
103928.m: The pelvis connects the spine with the legs.

103929.q: Which is the largest of the three parts of the hip bone?
103929.e: The ilium forms the wide, shovel-shaped upper half of the hip bone. It carries the iliac crest.
103929.m: The ilium is the large blade of the pelvis.

103930.q: How many bones make up the tarsus (the back of the foot)?
103930.e: The tarsus includes the talus, heel bone, navicular, cuboid and the cuneiform bones. Together that is seven bones.

103931.q: What is the joint between the talus and the heel bone called?
103931.e: The talus rests on the heel bone. The joint between them lets you tilt the foot inwards and outwards, for example on uneven ground.
103931.m: In the lower ankle joint, the foot tilts inwards and outwards.

103932.q: Which movement does the upper ankle joint between lower leg and foot mainly allow?
103932.e: The upper ankle joint works like a hinge. With it you can pull your foot up or point your toes down.
103932.m: In the upper ankle joint you raise and lower the foot.

103933.q: On which tarsal bone can a painful heel spur form?
103933.e: A heel spur is a small, thorn-like bony growth on the heel bone. It can hurt a lot when you step on it.
103933.m: A heel spur grows on the heel bone.

103934.q: Which bone connects the foot with the lower leg at the ankle?
103934.e: The talus lies at the top of the tarsus. With the tibia and fibula it forms the upper ankle joint.
103934.m: The talus connects the foot and the lower leg.

103935.q: How many bones does a human foot have, not counting tiny sesamoid bones?
103935.e: The tarsal bones are joined by 5 metatarsals and 14 toe bones. Altogether a foot has 26 bones.
103935.m: Each foot is made of 26 bones.

103936.q: Which tarsal bone is named after its shape and lies on the outer edge of the foot?
103936.e: The cuboid is roughly shaped like a cube. It lies on the outside in front of the heel bone and carries the outer metatarsals.
103936.m: The cuboid lies on the outer edge of the foot.

103937.q: Which is the largest bone of the tarsus?
103937.e: The heel bone forms the heel and is the largest bone of the foot. The Achilles tendon is attached to it.
103937.m: The heel bone is the largest foot bone.

103938.q: Which type of joint at the wrist lets you bring the thumb opposite the other fingers?
103938.e: The thumb joint at the wrist is a saddle joint. It lets the thumb tilt in two directions, so it can touch the fingertips and grip.
103938.m: The saddle joint makes the thumb so flexible.

103939.q: How do people especially often break a wrist bone?
a: By falling onto an outstretched hand
103939.e: If you fall and catch yourself with an outstretched hand, all your weight lands on the wrist. The scaphoid on the thumb side often breaks.
103939.m: Falling onto an outstretched hand can break a wrist bone.

103940.q: How many bones does a human hand have, not counting tiny sesamoid bones?
103940.e: A hand has 8 wrist bones, 5 metacarpals and 14 finger bones. Together that is 8 + 5 + 14 = 27.
103940.m: Each hand is made of 27 bones.

103942.q: Which wrist bone is named after a small pulse (a seed like peas and beans)?
103942.e: The pisiform is small and round like a pea. You can feel it on the little finger side of the heel of the hand.
103942.m: The small pisiform lies at the heel of the hand by the little finger.

103943.q: What runs through the carpal tunnel between the wrist bones and a ligament?
a: A nerve and the tendons of the finger flexors
103943.e: The wrist bones form a groove that a tight ligament closes into a tunnel. The median nerve and the flexor tendons of the fingers run through it.
103943.m: Tendons and an important nerve run through the carpal tunnel.

103944.q: Which wrist bone is named after a heavenly body?
103944.e: The lunate is shaped like a crescent moon. It lies in the first row between the scaphoid and the triquetrum.

103945.q: On an X-ray of the hand, how do doctors tell a child’s approximate bone age?
a: From the development of the wrist bones
From the colour of the fingernails
From the length of the hair
From the number of finger joints
103945.e: The wrist bones turn to bone one after another in a known order. From this the bone age can be estimated.
103945.m: On an X-ray, the wrist reveals the bone age.

a: Right at the top of the spine, just under the skull
Right at the bottom by the tailbone
In the middle of the back
At the front of the rib cage
103946.e: The atlas is the first neck vertebra. It carries the head and forms the upper head joint with the skull.
103946.m: The atlas is the top neck vertebra.

103947.q: Who is the atlas named after?
103947.e: In Greek myth the Titan Atlas carries the sky on his shoulders. The vertebra carries the head in the same way.
103947.m: The atlas carries the head as the Titan carried the sky.

103948.q: What does the atlas lack compared with most other vertebrae?
103948.e: The atlas is a ring of bone without a vertebral body. The part that would be its body has grown onto the second neck vertebra as a peg.
103948.m: The atlas is a ring without a vertebral body.

103949.q: How many neck vertebrae does a human have?
103949.e: Humans have seven neck vertebrae. The top one is the atlas, which carries the head.

103950.q: Which head movement does the joint between skull and atlas mainly allow?
103950.e: The upper head joint mainly lets the head tilt forwards and backwards. Turning happens further down.
103950.m: The upper head joint is the nodding joint.

103951.q: Which head movement does the joint between the atlas and the second neck vertebra mainly allow?
103951.e: The atlas turns with the skull around the peg of the second neck vertebra. That way you can turn your head left and right.
103951.m: The head turns between the atlas and the second neck vertebra.

103952.q: Which skull bone does the atlas form the upper head joint with?
103952.e: On two joint surfaces the atlas carries the knobs of the occipital bone. This joint lies right at the top of the spine.
103952.m: The atlas carries the occipital bone of the skull.

103953.q: What runs through the large hole in the ring of the atlas?
103953.e: As with all vertebrae, the ring of the atlas forms part of the spinal canal. The spinal cord runs safely inside it.
103953.m: The atlas protects the spinal cord just below the skull.

103954.q: How many fused vertebrae make up the sacrum?
103954.e: In adults, five sacral vertebrae fuse into a single bone. That is why this part of the spine cannot move.
103954.m: The sacrum is formed from five fused vertebrae.

a: A ring with a large hole
103955.e: The sacrum is wide at the top and narrows to a point at the bottom. It is also slightly curved backwards.
103955.m: The sacrum is an upside-down triangle of bone.

103956.q: Which section of the spine lies directly above the sacrum?
103956.e: Below the fifth lumbar vertebra comes the sacrum. There is still a disc between the two.
103956.m: The sacrum lies below the last lumbar vertebra.

103957.q: Where in the body is the sacrum?
a: In the lower back between the hip bones
In the neck under the skull
At the front of the chest by the heart
In the lower leg next to the tibia
103957.e: The sacrum sits at the lower end of the spine. It is wedged between the two hip bones and so is also part of the pelvis.
103957.m: The sacrum lies in the lower back between the hip bones.

103958.q: What lies directly below the sacrum, at the very bottom of the spine?
103958.e: Below the sacrum comes the small tailbone. It is what is left of a tail that our ancestors once had.
103958.m: The tailbone sits below the sacrum.

103959.q: What are the holes in the sacrum for?
103959.e: Nerves leave the spinal canal through the holes in the sacrum. Among other things, they supply the legs and bottom.
103959.m: Nerves to the legs pass through the holes in the sacrum.

103960.q: What job does the sacrum do in the skeleton?
a: It connects the spine with the pelvis
It protects the heart from the front
It forms the floor of the eye socket
It connects the upper arm and forearm
103960.e: The sacrum is wedged between the two hip bones. Through it, the weight of the upper body passes to the pelvis.
103960.m: The sacrum carries the spine and is firmly anchored in the pelvis.

103961.q: Why can’t the sacrum move, unlike the lumbar vertebrae?
a: Its vertebrae have fused into one bone
It is made only of cartilage
It is connected to the skull
103961.e: In adults the five sacral vertebrae have fused into a single solid bone. That is why they can no longer move against each other.
103961.m: The sacrum is rigid because its vertebrae are fused.

103962.q: What is special about the hyoid bone?
a: It has no joint with any other bone
It is the largest bone in the head
It is made only of cartilage
It keeps growing into old age
103962.e: The hyoid is only held in place by muscles and ligaments. It is the only bone with no joint connecting it to another bone.
103962.m: The hyoid floats in muscles and ligaments without a joint.

a: In the neck above the larynx
In the palate above the tongue
In the back of the neck behind the atlas
In the chest behind the breastbone
103963.e: The hyoid lies at the front of the neck between the lower jaw and the larynx. You can feel it just above the Adam’s apple.
103963.m: The hyoid lies at the front of the neck above the larynx.

103964.q: What shape is the hyoid bone?
103964.e: The hyoid is curved like a horseshoe. Its body is at the front and its ends point backwards.
103964.m: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone.

103965.q: For which activities does the hyoid bone play an important role?
103965.e: Muscles of the tongue, the floor of the mouth and the larynx are attached to the hyoid. They work together when the mouth and throat move.
103965.m: The hyoid helps with swallowing and speaking.

103966.q: Which organ is attached to the hyoid bone by muscles?
103966.e: The tongue is anchored to the hyoid by its muscles. That is why in German the bone is called the “tongue bone”.
103966.m: The tongue is anchored to the hyoid.

103967.q: What do you feel when you put your fingers on the front of your neck while swallowing?
103967.e: When you swallow, muscles pull the hyoid and larynx up and forwards. This covers the windpipe so nothing gets into it.
103967.m: When you swallow, the hyoid rises with the larynx.

103968.q: What holds the hyoid bone in place in the neck?
103968.e: The hyoid has no joint with any other bone. It hangs only from muscles and ligaments between the lower jaw and the larynx.
103968.m: The hyoid hangs from muscles and ligaments.

103969.q: Why is the hyoid bone important for speaking?
a: The tongue and larynx are anchored to it
It warms the air you breathe
103969.e: Muscles of the tongue and larynx are attached to the hyoid. That way the tongue and larynx can move precisely when you speak.
103969.m: The hyoid gives the tongue and larynx something to hold on to.

103970.q: How do the radius and ulna lie when your palm faces up?
a: Stacked on top of each other
103970.e: When the palm faces up, the radius lies parallel next to the ulna. When you turn the hand down, the radius crosses over the ulna.
103970.m: With the palm facing up, the radius and ulna lie parallel.

103971.q: How many bones does the upper arm have?
103971.e: There is only the humerus in the upper arm. In the forearm, on the other hand, there are two bones, the ulna and the radius.
103971.m: The upper arm has only one bone.

103972.q: Which tarsal bone lies on the inside between the talus and the cuneiforms and is named after a boat?
103972.e: The navicular bone of the foot is curved like a little boat. It lies at the inner arch of the foot in front of the talus.
103972.m: The foot has a boat-shaped navicular bone.

a: Between the forearm and the palm
103973.e: The wrist forms the link between the forearm and the hand. Its 8 small bones make the wrist flexible.
103973.m: The wrist connects the forearm and the hand.

103974.q: A bicycle travels 15 km in 30 minutes. What is its speed?
103974.e: 30 minutes are 0.5 h. v = 15 km ÷ 0.5 h = 30 km/h.
103974.m: You first have to convert minutes into hours.

103975.q: A bus covers 90 km in 1.5 hours. What is its average speed?
103975.m: You divide the distance by the time taken.

103976.q: A dog runs at 5 m/s for 12 seconds. How far does it get?

103977.q: How long does a pedestrian take to cover 450 m if she walks at 1.5 m/s?
103977.e: t = s ÷ v = 450 m ÷ 1.5 m/s = 300 s, which is 5 minutes.
103977.m: Time is distance divided by speed.

103978.q: In physics, what also belongs to velocity besides its size?
103978.e: Velocity is a quantity with a direction (a vector). If the direction changes, the velocity changes too, even at the same speed.
103978.m: Velocity has a size and a direction.

103979.q: In shipping, which unit is usually used for the speed of ships?
103979.e: A knot is one nautical mile per hour, which is 1.852 km/h. The unit is also used in aviation.
103979.m: Ships measure their speed in knots.

103980.q: A car travels 180 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
103980.m: Half hours count towards the travel time too.

103981.q: Lea drives a route there at 60 km/h and the same distance back at 40 km/h. What is her average speed?
103981.e: For a 120 km route she needs 2 h there and 3 h back. 240 km ÷ 5 h = 48 km/h. Because she drives slowly for longer, the value is below 50 km/h.
103981.m: You can't simply take the average of the speeds.

103982.q: A 12 km hike takes 4 hours in total, including a one-hour break. What is the average speed including the break?
103982.e: Total distance 12 km, total time 4 h, so 12 km ÷ 4 h = 3 km/h. The break counts too.

103983.q: A runner sprints 100 m in 12.5 seconds. What is her average speed?
103983.m: For sprints you usually calculate in metres per second.

103984.q: A train travels for 1 h at 120 km/h, stops for 30 min and then travels for 30 min at 60 km/h. What is the average speed?
103984.e: Distance: 120 km + 30 km = 150 km. Time: 1 h + 0.5 h + 0.5 h = 2 h. 150 km ÷ 2 h = 75 km/h.
103984.m: The stopping time is part of the total time too.

103985.q: The way to school is 1.2 km long, and Nico takes 15 minutes. What is his average walking speed?
103985.e: 15 minutes are 0.25 h. 1.2 km ÷ 0.25 h = 4.8 km/h.
103985.m: A quarter of an hour is 0.25 hours.

103986.q: What does an average speed check measure, where the police record the time between two measuring points?
103986.e: The known distance between the measuring points and the time taken give the average speed. Anyone who drives too fast in between is caught this way.
103986.m: In an average speed check, the speed over the whole stretch counts.

103987.q: A runner completes the marathon (42.195 km) in 3 hours. Roughly what was his average speed?
103987.m: In a marathon what counts is a steady pace over a long time.

103988.q: What is meant by instantaneous speed?
a: The speed at one particular moment
The average speed of a whole journey
103988.e: Instantaneous speed tells you how fast an object is moving right now. It can change from moment to moment.
103988.m: Instantaneous speed only applies to one moment.

103989.q: Which speed does a car's speedometer show?
a: The speed relative to the wind
The top speed of the journey
103989.e: The speedometer constantly measures how fast the wheels are turning at that moment and shows the current speed.
103989.m: The speedometer shows the speed at this very moment.

103990.q: What is the instantaneous speed of a ball thrown straight up at its highest point?
a: Half as much as when thrown
103990.e: The ball gets slower and slower as it rises. At the highest point it turns round and stands still for a moment.
103990.m: At the turning point the speed is briefly zero.

103991.q: A stone falls without air resistance, and its speed increases by about 9.8 m/s every second. How fast is it after 3 seconds?
103991.e: v = 9.8 m/s per second · 3 s = 29.4 m/s.
103991.m: In free fall the speed increases by the same amount every second.

103992.q: Where is the instantaneous speed of a swinging pendulum greatest?
a: At the highest point on the left
At the highest point on the right
103992.e: At the turning points the pendulum briefly stands still. On the way down it gets faster and reaches its greatest speed at the lowest point.
103992.m: A pendulum is fastest at the bottom.

103993.q: A car takes 0.2 seconds to pass a 4 m measuring section. Roughly how fast is it going at that moment?
103993.e: 4 m ÷ 0.2 s = 20 m/s. 20 m/s · 3.6 = 72 km/h. With such a short measuring time this is almost the instantaneous speed.
103993.m: The shorter the measuring time, the more accurately you get the instantaneous speed.

103994.q: When is the instantaneous speed always equal to the average speed?
a: When going round a bend while braking
103994.e: In uniform motion the speed never changes. So at every moment it is the same as the average.
103994.m: At constant speed, instantaneous and average speed are the same.

103995.q: How can you tell the instantaneous speed at a certain time from a distance-time graph?
a: From the gradient of the curve at that point
From the height of the curve at that point
From the area under the curve
From the length of the time axis
103995.e: The gradient of the tangent at a point tells you how fast the distance is changing there at that moment. That is the instantaneous speed.
103995.m: The gradient of a distance-time graph reveals the speed at that moment.

103996.q: What is usually plotted on the horizontal axis of a distance-time graph?
103996.e: Time goes on the horizontal axis and the distance covered on the vertical one. That way you can see where an object is at any time.
103996.m: In a distance-time graph, time runs to the right.

103997.q: What does a straight line sloping upwards in a distance-time graph mean?
a: An object getting faster and faster
103997.e: In equal times, equal numbers of metres are added. That is why the line is straight.
103997.m: A sloping straight line shows a constant speed.

103998.q: What does a horizontal line in a distance-time graph mean?
a: The object is moving very fast
103998.e: Time goes on, but the distance stays the same. So the object is not moving.
103998.m: A horizontal line means standing still.

103999.q: Two straight lines in a distance-time graph rise at different slopes. What does the steeper line mean?
103999.e: With the steeper line, more distance is added in the same time. So the object is faster.
103999.m: The steeper the line, the faster the movement.

104000.q: A straight line in a distance-time graph goes from 0 m at 0 s to 50 m at 10 s. What is the speed?
104000.m: The gradient of the line is the speed.

104001.q: A straight line in a distance-time graph goes from 20 m at 0 s to 60 m at 4 s. What is the speed?
104001.e: In 4 s, 60 m minus 20 m = 40 m is added. v = 40 m ÷ 4 s = 10 m/s.
104001.m: You divide the change in distance by the time it took.

104002.q: What does a line in a distance-time graph that slopes downwards to the right mean?
a: The object is moving back towards the starting point
104002.e: The distance from the starting point gets smaller over time. So the object is moving back.
104002.m: A falling line means moving back towards the start.

104003.q: What does a curve in a distance-time graph that keeps getting steeper show?
104003.e: The gradient increases, so more and more distance is added each second. The object is getting faster.
104003.m: A curve that keeps getting steeper shows increasing speed.

104004.q: What does it mean when the lines of two cyclists cross in a distance-time graph?
a: Both are at the same place at the same time
Both are going at the same speed
Both are going in opposite directions
104004.e: The crossing point has the same time and the same distance for both. That is where they meet or one overtakes the other.
104004.m: A crossing point shows a meeting point.

104005.q: What is typical of uniform motion in a straight line?
a: Constant speed in the same direction
The same speed on a circular path
104005.e: In uniform motion in a straight line, neither the size nor the direction of the velocity changes.
104005.m: Uniform motion has a constant speed.

104006.q: Which formula gives the distance in uniform motion?
104006.e: At constant speed the distance grows evenly with time. The distance is speed multiplied by time.
104006.m: At constant speed you multiply speed and time.

104007.q: A toy car moves uniformly at 3 m/s. How far does it get in 7 seconds?
104007.m: Every second the same distance is added.

104008.q: What does the speed-time graph of uniform motion look like?
104008.e: The speed stays the same at every moment. That is why the line is horizontal.
104008.m: Constant speed gives a horizontal line on a speed-time graph.

104009.q: In uniform motion, what happens to the distance if you double the time?
104009.e: At constant speed, distance and time are proportional. Double the time means double the distance.
104009.m: In uniform motion, distance and time are proportional.

104010.q: According to Newton's first law, what is true of the forces on an object moving uniformly in a straight line?
104010.e: With no resultant force, an object stays at rest or carries on moving uniformly in a straight line. This is called the principle of inertia.
104010.m: With no resultant force, the speed stays the same.

104011.q: A passenger boat on Lake Zurich travels uniformly at 24 km/h. How far does it get in 45 minutes?
104011.e: 45 minutes are 0.75 h. s = 24 km/h · 0.75 h = 18 km.
104011.m: You count minutes as a fraction of an hour.

104012.q: A snail crawls uniformly at 1.5 mm/s. How long does it take to cover 9 cm?
104012.e: 9 cm are 90 mm. t = 90 mm ÷ 1.5 mm/s = 60 s.
104012.m: Before calculating, put distance and speed in the same unit of length.

104013.q: Which example comes closest to uniform motion?
a: A car pulling away at traffic lights
104013.e: An escalator runs at a constant speed in one direction. The other examples get faster or slower.

104014.q: What is the SI unit of speed?
104014.e: In the International System of Units (SI), speed is given in m/s. km/h is common in everyday life but is not an SI unit.
104014.m: The SI unit of speed is metres per second.

104015.q: What does a speed of 1 m/s mean?
a: It takes an hour to cover 1 m
104015.e: Metres per second means this many metres in one second. At 1 m/s it is exactly one metre per second.
104015.m: Metres per second tells you how many metres you cover in one second.

104016.q: In 2009 Usain Bolt ran the 100 m in 9.58 s (world record as of 2026). Roughly what was his average speed?
104016.e: v = 100 m ÷ 9.58 s ≈ 10.44 m/s, which is about 37.6 km/h.
104016.m: World-class sprinters manage over ten metres per second.

104017.q: A ball rolls at 4 m/s. How far does it get in half a second?
104017.m: In half a second you get half as far as in a whole one.

104018.q: How long does a cyclist take to cover 1 km if she rides at 5 m/s?
104018.m: You first have to convert kilometres into metres.

104019.q: An object moves at 0.5 m/s. How many centimetres does it cover in one second?
104019.e: 0.5 m/s means 0.5 m every second. 0.5 m is 50 cm.
104019.m: Half a metre per second is 50 centimetres every second.

104020.q: A conveyor belt moves parcels at 3 m/s. How far does a parcel get in one minute?
104020.e: A minute has 60 s. s = 3 m/s · 60 s = 180 m.
104020.m: You have to count a minute as 60 seconds.

104021.q: Which number do you divide a speed in km/h by to convert it into m/s?
104021.e: 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s = 1/3.6 m/s. That is why you divide by 3.6.
104021.m: From km/h to m/s you divide by 3.6.

104022.q: How much is 90 km/h in m/s?
104022.m: At 90 km/h you cover 25 metres every second.

104023.q: A gale blows at 15 m/s. How much is that in km/h?
104023.e: From m/s to km/h you multiply by 3.6: 15 · 3.6 = 54 km/h.
104023.m: From m/s to km/h you multiply by 3.6.

104024.q: How much is 108 km/h in m/s?
104024.m: At 108 km/h you cover 30 metres every second.

104025.q: How much is 144 km/h in m/s?
104025.m: At 144 km/h you cover 40 metres every second.

104026.q: Which is faster: 20 m/s or 60 km/h?
104026.e: 20 m/s · 3.6 = 72 km/h. That is more than 60 km/h.
104026.m: To compare, convert both values into the same unit.

104027.q: Why is the conversion factor between km/h and m/s exactly 3.6?
a: 1 h has 3600 s and 1 km has 1000 m
1 h has 360 s and 1 km has 100 m
104027.m: The factor 3.6 comes from 3600 seconds and 1000 metres.

104028.q: Outside built-up areas in Switzerland the limit is usually 80. Roughly how much is 80 km/h in m/s?
104028.m: At 80 km/h you cover over 20 metres every second.

104029.q: An aeroplane flies at 250 m/s. How much is that in km/h?
104029.m: Passenger planes fly at about 900 kilometres per hour.

104030.q: What is a frame of reference in physics?
a: The point of view from which you describe a movement
A road sign for speed limits
A list of all units of measurement
104030.e: Whether and how fast something moves depends on what you compare it with. The chosen frame of reference fixes this point of view with a zero point and directions.
104030.m: Every movement is described in a chosen frame of reference.

104031.q: Mia is sitting in a moving train. Is she at rest or moving?
a: It depends on the frame of reference
104031.e: Seen from the train, Mia is sitting still. Seen from the platform, she is moving with the train.
104031.m: Rest and motion are always relative.

104032.q: In everyday life, what are you usually comparing with when you say a car is going at 50 km/h?
104032.e: In everyday life the Earth's surface, meaning roads and houses, is usually chosen as the frame of reference. The speedometer also measures the speed relative to the road.
104032.m: In everyday life the Earth's surface is the usual frame of reference.

104033.q: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky every day?
a: Because the Earth turns on its axis
Because the Sun circles the Earth
Because the Sun spins on itself
Because the air moves the Sun
104033.e: We are watching from the turning Earth. In this frame of reference the Sun seems to move from east to west.
104033.m: The Sun's apparent movement comes from the Earth's rotation.

104034.q: Why does a geostationary TV satellite seem to stand still in the sky?
a: It circles the Earth as fast as the Earth turns
It is exactly above the North Pole
104034.e: A geostationary satellite takes exactly as long to go round once as the Earth takes to turn once on its axis, just under 24 hours. Seen from the Earth, it therefore always stays in the same place.
104034.m: A geostationary satellite is at rest in the Earth's frame of reference.

104035.q: At the station the train next to you pulls away, and you think your own train is moving. Why?
a: You unconsciously use the other train as your frame of reference
Your own train rolls back slightly
104035.e: If you can only see the train next to you, there is no fixed point of reference. Your brain then can't tell which train is moving.
104035.m: Without a fixed point of reference, you are easily fooled about movement.

104036.q: A point on the equator is moved by the Earth's rotation. Roughly how fast is it, if the Earth's circumference is about 40,075 km?
104036.e: In 24 hours it covers the Earth's circumference once: 40,075 km ÷ 24 h ≈ 1670 km/h. We feel nothing of it because we are moving along with it.
104036.m: We turn with the Earth without noticing.

104037.q: Two cars are driving in the same direction, one at 100 km/h and one at 80 km/h. How fast is the faster one catching up with the slower one?
104037.e: In the same direction you subtract the speeds: 100 minus 80 = 20 km/h.
104037.m: In the same direction, the relative speed is the difference.

104038.q: Two cars are driving towards each other, one at 100 km/h and one at 80 km/h. What is their relative speed?
104038.e: In opposite directions you add the speeds: 100 + 80 = 180 km/h.
104038.m: With oncoming traffic, the speeds add up.

104039.q: A train is travelling at 100 km/h. A child inside walks forwards at 5 km/h. How fast is the child moving relative to the ground?
104039.e: The child moves with the train and also forwards: 100 + 5 = 105 km/h.
104039.m: Speeds in the same direction add up.

104040.q: A train is travelling at 100 km/h. A child inside walks backwards at 5 km/h. How fast is the child moving relative to the ground?
104040.e: The child walks against the direction of travel: 100 minus 5 = 95 km/h.
104040.m: Speeds in opposite directions are subtracted.

104041.q: A 30 m long escalator moves at 0.5 m/s. A man walks up it at 1 m/s. How long does he take?
104041.e: Relative to the ground he moves at 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 m/s. t = 30 m ÷ 1.5 m/s = 20 s.
104041.m: On an escalator your own speed adds to the speed of the escalator.

104042.q: A boat moves through the water at 5 m/s against a current of 2 m/s. How fast does it make progress relative to the bank?
104042.e: The current slows the boat down: 5 minus 2 = 3 m/s.
104042.m: Against the current, a boat makes slower progress.

104043.q: Two trains are 150 km apart and travel towards each other at 70 km/h and 80 km/h. After how long do they meet?
104043.e: The gap between them shrinks by 70 + 80 = 150 km every hour. 150 km ÷ 150 km/h = 1 h.
104043.m: With oncoming traffic, the gap shrinks by the sum of the speeds.

104044.q: A car at 30 m/s overtakes a lorry at 25 m/s and has to gain 50 m to do so. How long does the overtaking take?
104044.e: The car is only 30 minus 25 = 5 m/s faster than the lorry. t = 50 m ÷ 5 m/s = 10 s.
104044.m: When overtaking, only the difference in speed counts.

104045.q: Why do raindrops run diagonally across the window of a moving train, even though the rain is falling straight down?
a: Because the train is moving relative to the rain
Because there is wind inside the train
Because water falls at an angle
104045.e: Seen from the train, a backwards movement is added to the falling movement of the drop. Together that makes a diagonal path.
104045.m: What you see depends on your own movement.

a: The time from noticing a danger to acting
The time from braking to stopping
The time for a whole journey
The time until the next traffic lights
104046.e: First you have to see the danger, understand it and decide. Only then do you, for example, press the brake.
104046.m: Reaction time passes before you even act.

104047.q: Which reaction time is often used as a rule of thumb in road traffic?
104047.e: For drivers you often reckon with about one second. Depending on how alert they are, it can be shorter or much longer.
104047.m: In traffic you reckon with about one second of reaction time.

104048.q: How does a car move during the driver's reaction time?
a: It carries on at the same speed
104048.e: During the reaction time the driver has not yet braked. The car carries on at its previous speed and covers the thinking distance.
104048.m: During the reaction time the car carries on without braking.

104049.q: A car is going at 50 km/h and the reaction time is 1 s. Roughly how long is the thinking distance?
104049.m: At 50 km/h you travel almost 14 metres in one second of reaction time.

104050.q: A car is going at 100 km/h and the reaction time is 1 s. Roughly how long is the thinking distance?
104050.m: At high speed even the thinking distance becomes long.

104051.q: What makes the reaction time behind the wheel much longer?
a: Being distracted by a mobile phone
104051.e: Anyone looking at their phone notices a danger later. Tiredness, alcohol and drugs also make the reaction time longer.
104051.m: If you are distracted, you react too late.

104053.q: In top-level sport, below what reaction time after the starting gun does a sprint start count as a false start?
104053.e: Starting blocks measure the pressure of the feet. According to the rules, anyone who reacts faster than 0.1 s after the gun cannot have been reacting to the gun.
104053.m: Nobody reacts faster than about a tenth of a second.

104054.q: How does the thinking distance change if you drive twice as fast?
a: It becomes four times as long
104054.e: Thinking distance is speed times reaction time. With the same reaction time it grows in proportion to the speed.
104054.m: Thinking distance grows in the same proportion as the speed.

104055.q: Roughly how does the braking distance change if you drive twice as fast?
a: It becomes four times as long
It becomes eight times as long
104055.e: Braking distance grows with the square of the speed: s = v² ÷ (2a). Double the speed gives 2 · 2 = 4 times the braking distance.
104055.m: Braking distance grows with the square of the speed.

104056.q: Roughly how does the braking distance change if you drive three times as fast?
a: It becomes nine times as long
It becomes three times as long
It becomes six times as long
104056.e: Because braking distance grows with v², three times the speed gives 3 · 3 = 9 times the braking distance.
104056.m: Even a little more speed makes the braking distance much longer.

104059.q: At 30 km/h a car has a braking distance of 4.5 m. How long is it under the same conditions at 60 km/h?
104059.e: Double the speed gives four times the braking distance: 4.5 m · 4 = 18 m.
104059.m: At double the speed you need four times as much room to brake.

104060.q: A car is going at 20 m/s and brakes evenly at 5 m/s². How long does it take to come to a stop?
104060.e: Every second the car loses 5 m/s. t = 20 m/s ÷ 5 m/s² = 4 s.
104060.m: Braking time is speed divided by deceleration.

104061.q: Why is the braking distance on ice much longer than on a dry road?
a: The tyres grip much worse on ice
Reaction time is longer on ice
There is no gravity on ice
104061.e: On ice the static friction between tyres and road is very small. That is why the car can only brake weakly.
104061.m: On ice and snow you need much more room to brake.

104062.q: What makes up the stopping distance?
104062.e: First the car carries on without braking during the reaction time, then it brakes until it stops. Both distances together make the stopping distance.
