104062.m: Stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance.

104063.q: The thinking distance is 14 m and the braking distance 12 m. How long is the stopping distance?
104063.e: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance = 14 m + 12 m = 26 m.
104063.m: For the stopping distance you add both distances together.

104066.q: At 36 km/h, by how much does the stopping distance increase if the reaction time is 2 s instead of 1 s because of a distraction?
104066.e: 36 km/h = 10 m/s. One second more reaction time means 10 m/s · 1 s = 10 m more distance. The braking distance stays the same.
104066.m: Every second of distraction makes the stopping distance longer.

104070.q: Which part of the stopping distance does not depend on the brakes and the state of the road?
104070.e: During the reaction time there is no braking yet. The thinking distance depends only on the speed and the reaction time.
104070.m: The thinking distance happens before the brakes work.

104071.q: A passenger drops a ball in a train travelling steadily in a straight line. From his point of view, where does the ball land?
a: Far behind him in the carriage
Far in front of him in the carriage
On the ceiling of the carriage
104071.e: Even before being let go, the ball is moving along with the train and keeps this speed. In the train's frame of reference it therefore falls straight down.
104071.m: In a train moving uniformly, things fall just as in a room at rest.

104072.q: A scientist planted a willow in a pot of weighed soil. After five years the tree was much heavier, but the soil was hardly any lighter. What did this show?
a: Plants don't simply grow out of the soil
104072.e: Jan Baptist van Helmont's willow experiment showed that the mass of the plant does not come from the soil. Today we know that it is built up mainly from carbon dioxide and water.
104072.m: The willow experiment showed that plants don't simply grow out of soil.

104073.q: What does a plant mainly build up its mass from?
104073.e: In 1804 the Geneva scientist Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure showed that plants take in carbon from the air and parts of water. The soil only supplies a few minerals.
104073.m: Plants are built up mainly from air and water.

104074.q: Which plant organ is the most important site of photosynthesis?
104074.e: Leaves are flat and have a large surface area to catch lots of light. Their cells contain especially many chloroplasts.
104074.m: The leaf is the factory of photosynthesis.

104075.q: What does the Greek word part “photo” in the word photosynthesis mean?
104075.e: In Greek, “phos” means light and “synthesis” means putting together. So photosynthesis means building up with the help of light.
104075.m: Photosynthesis means building up with light.

104076.q: What are plants called in a food chain, because they make their own nutrients through photosynthesis?
104076.e: Plants make energy-rich substances from light, water and carbon dioxide. All other living things in a food chain depend on them directly or indirectly.
104076.m: Green plants are the producers in the food chain.

104077.q: Which gas do leaves take in from the air for photosynthesis?
104077.e: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through the stomata and give off oxygen. The Geneva naturalist Jean Senebier already recognised this in the 18th century.
104077.m: Leaves take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen.

104078.q: What is the green pigment that captures light in photosynthesis called?
104078.e: Chlorophyll is in the chloroplasts of plant cells. It captures the energy of light and makes leaves green.
104078.m: Chlorophyll captures the light for photosynthesis.

104079.q: Where does a plant get the energy for photosynthesis from?
104079.e: Photosynthesis needs light energy. With it, the plant builds up sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
104079.m: The energy for photosynthesis comes from light.

104080.q: Why is plant photosynthesis vital for humans and animals too?
104080.e: Almost all food comes from plants, either directly or via animals. In addition, the oxygen we breathe comes from photosynthesis.
104080.m: Without photosynthesis there would be neither enough food nor oxygen to breathe.

104081.q: Which solvent is used in a school experiment to dissolve chlorophyll out of crushed leaves?
104081.e: Chlorophyll hardly dissolves in water, but dissolves well in alcohol such as ethanol. This makes the extract bright green.
104081.m: Chlorophyll dissolves in alcohol, not in water.

104082.q: Which colours of light does chlorophyll absorb especially well?
104082.e: The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll has two peaks, one in the blue range and one in the red range. The plant uses this light energy for photosynthesis.
104082.m: Chlorophyll mainly uses red and blue light.

104083.q: Which metal atom sits in the middle of a chlorophyll molecule?
104083.e: A magnesium atom is bound in the centre of the ring-shaped chlorophyll molecule. If a plant lacks magnesium, its leaves turn yellowish.
104083.m: At the heart of chlorophyll there is a magnesium atom.

104084.q: Why do many leaves turn yellow and orange in autumn?
a: The leaves take in pigment from the soil
The frost colours the leaf cells
104084.e: Before the leaves fall, the tree breaks down the valuable chlorophyll and takes back its building blocks. Then yellow and orange pigments become visible that were previously hidden by the green.
104084.m: In autumn the green disappears and other leaf colours appear.

104085.q: What does the word “chlorophyll”, which comes from Greek, mean?
104085.e: “Chloros” means green or yellowish green, and “phyllon” means leaf. So chlorophyll literally means leaf green.

104086.q: Which pigment in human blood is the chlorophyll molecule similar to in structure?
104086.e: Both molecules have a similar ring-shaped framework. But haemoglobin has iron in the middle, while chlorophyll has a different metal.
104086.m: Leaf green and the red blood pigment have a similar ring framework.

104087.q: What are the yellow to orange accessory pigments in leaves that are also found in carrots called?
104087.e: Carotenoids help to capture light and protect chlorophyll from too much light. The name comes from the carrot.
104087.m: Carotenoids are yellow and orange leaf pigments.

104088.q: What do seedlings need in order to form green chlorophyll?
104088.e: Seedlings that grow in the dark stay pale and yellowish. Only in the light do they form chlorophyll and turn green.
104088.m: Plants need light to turn green.

104089.q: Where does a land plant get the carbon dioxide for photosynthesis from?
104089.e: Carbon dioxide is part of the air. It gets inside the leaf through tiny openings in the leaf's skin.
104089.m: Plants get their carbon dioxide from the air.

104090.q: What is the chemical formula of carbon dioxide?
104090.e: A carbon dioxide molecule consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. CO, on the other hand, is poisonous carbon monoxide.
104090.m: Carbon dioxide has the formula CO2.

104091.q: Roughly what proportion of the air is carbon dioxide (as of 2026)?
104091.e: Today the air contains around 430 parts of CO2 per million parts, which is about 0.04 per cent. Despite this small proportion, it is enough for photosynthesis.
104091.m: Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent of the air.

104092.q: What happens to the carbon from carbon dioxide during photosynthesis?
a: It is given off again as a gas
104092.e: The plant builds the carbon atoms into sugar molecules. In this way a gas becomes a solid building material of the plant.
104092.m: In photosynthesis, carbon is built into sugar.

104093.q: Why are forests considered carbon stores?
a: Trees lock up carbon in their wood
Trees only give off carbon dioxide
Trees store gas in their roots
104093.e: Over decades, trees take in carbon dioxide and build the carbon into wood. Only when the wood rots or burns is it released again.
104093.m: A lot of carbon is stored in the wood of trees.

104094.q: Why is extra carbon dioxide added to the air in some greenhouses?
104094.e: When there is a lot of light, carbon dioxide is often the limiting factor of photosynthesis. More CO2 in the greenhouse air can therefore increase yields.
104094.m: More carbon dioxide can boost plant growth in the greenhouse.

104095.q: Which gas is heavier than air and therefore collects on the floor of wine cellars during fermentation?
104095.e: When grape juice ferments, a lot of carbon dioxide is produced. Because it is heavier than air, it can collect on the floor of cellars and become dangerous.
104095.m: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects at the bottom.

104097.q: Which test is used to detect oxygen in a test tube?
104097.e: If you hold a glowing wooden splint in oxygen, it bursts brightly into flame. Oxygen strongly supports burning.
104097.m: A glowing splint that bursts into flame shows oxygen.

104098.q: Roughly what proportion of the air is oxygen?
104098.e: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen and about 21 per cent oxygen. The rest is mainly argon and carbon dioxide.
104098.m: About a fifth of the air is oxygen.

104099.q: How can you make oxygen production visible in a water plant such as Canadian waterweed?
104099.e: In light, small gas bubbles that contain a lot of oxygen rise from the waterweed. The more bubbles, the stronger the photosynthesis.
104099.m: Rising bubbles on waterweed show photosynthesis.

104100.q: Where does the oxygen in the air that we breathe come from?
a: From plants, algae and bacteria that carry out photosynthesis
104100.e: Over 2 billion years ago, tiny bacteria in the sea began to give off oxygen. Today plants, algae and these bacteria supply the oxygen in the air.
104100.m: The oxygen in the air comes from photosynthesis.

104101.q: What did a famous experiment with a candle, a sprig of a plant and a glass bell jar show?
a: Plants make used air breathable again
Plants only grow in the dark
104101.e: Around 1771, Joseph Priestley let a candle burn out under a glass bell jar. With a sprig of mint inside, the air could afterwards keep a flame burning again.

104103.q: What is glucose also called in everyday life?
104103.e: Glucose was first obtained from grapes. That is where the name grape sugar comes from.
104103.m: Glucose is also called grape sugar.

104104.q: What else is glucose known as?
104104.e: Glucose is also known as grape sugar or dextrose. It is found in fruit and is an important source of energy.

104105.q: Table sugar is made of two building blocks. Which is one of them?
104105.e: Table sugar consists of one unit each of glucose and fructose. It is obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane.
104105.m: Table sugar consists of glucose and fructose.

104106.q: Which building material of the plant cell wall is made of glucose units?
104106.e: Cellulose consists of long chains of glucose units. It makes cell walls sturdy and is the main component of wood and paper.
104106.m: Cellulose is a cell wall material made of glucose.

104107.q: What does a plant mainly use the glucose from photosynthesis for?
a: As a source of energy and building material
104107.e: The plant gets energy for its life processes from glucose. It also uses it to build other substances such as cellulose, fats and proteins.
104107.m: For the plant, glucose is both a source of energy and a building material.

104108.q: Which group of substances does glucose belong to?
104108.e: Glucose is a simple sugar. Sugars and the substances built from them belong to the group of carbohydrates.

104109.q: Which hormone lowers the glucose level in human blood?
104109.e: Insulin is made in the pancreas. It makes body cells take up glucose from the blood.

104110.q: What is starch used for in plants?
104110.e: Plants make sugar during photosynthesis. Whatever they don't need straight away, they store as starch, for example in tubers and seeds.
104110.m: Starch is the energy store of plants.

104111.q: What colour appears when iodine solution meets starch?
104111.e: Iodine fits into the spiral-shaped starch chains. This produces a deep blue to black colour.

104112.q: In which part does the potato plant store especially a lot of starch?
104112.e: The potato tuber is a swollen underground shoot. The plant uses it as a store for starch.
104112.m: Potatoes store starch in their tubers.

104113.q: Which group of sugars does starch belong to?
104113.e: Starch consists of very many linked sugar units. Such giant molecules are called polysaccharides.

104114.q: Why do plants usually store sugar as starch and not as dissolved sugar?
104114.e: Starch is hardly soluble in water and therefore doesn't draw water into the cell. That way a lot of energy can be stored in little space.
104114.m: Starch is a space-saving, barely soluble energy store.

104115.q: A leaf is partly covered with aluminium foil and exposed to light. Which part does not change colour in the iodine test afterwards?
a: Only the tip of the leaf
104115.e: Only where light reached could photosynthesis take place and starch form. The covered part stays pale in the iodine test.
104115.m: Only parts of a leaf exposed to light form starch.

104116.q: Which food consists largely of starch?
104116.e: Wheat grains store a lot of starch in the endosperm as a reserve for the embryo. That is why flour consists mostly of starch.
104116.m: Flour contains a lot of starch.

104117.q: Which tropical plant provides a staple food for many millions of people with its starchy root tubers?
104117.e: Cassava grows in Africa, South America and Asia. Its tubers contain a lot of starch and are cooked or made into flour.
104117.m: Cassava is an important starchy tuber crop of the tropics.

104119.q: Into which form of energy does a plant convert light energy during photosynthesis?
104119.e: The energy of light is stored in the bonds of the sugar molecules. This is chemical energy.
104119.m: Plants convert light energy into chemical energy.

104120.q: Which light do plants mainly use for photosynthesis?
104120.e: Plants mainly use the light that we can see too. They absorb red and blue light especially well.

104121.q: What happens to photosynthesis when the light intensity increases from very weak to medium?
104121.e: In weak light, light is the limiting factor. More light then means more photosynthesis.
104121.m: In weak light, more light increases photosynthesis.

104122.q: Why does photosynthesis eventually stop increasing in very strong light?
a: The leaves reflect all the light
The plant rests during the day
104122.e: When there is a lot of light, other factors such as carbon dioxide or temperature become the bottleneck. The curve therefore levels off.
104122.m: In very bright light, other factors limit photosynthesis.

104123.q: What does a plant keep doing even in total darkness?
104123.e: Without light, photosynthesis is not possible. But the plant respires day and night, using up sugar and oxygen.
104123.m: Plants respire in the dark too.

104124.q: What are plants called that manage with little light and grow on the forest floor, for example?
104124.e: Shade plants often have large, thin leaves and make good use of weak light. Examples are many ferns and wood sorrel.
104124.m: Shade plants manage with little light.

104125.q: Where does the energy stored in coal, oil and natural gas ultimately come from?
104125.e: These fuels formed from the remains of living things that lived millions of years ago. Their energy came from sunlight through photosynthesis.
104125.m: Coal, oil and natural gas contain stored solar energy.

104126.q: What is the growth of a plant towards light called?
104126.e: Plants grow more on the shady side of the shoot. This makes the shoot bend towards the light, for example in plants by a window.
104126.m: Thanks to phototropism, plants grow towards the light.

104127.q: In which cell parts does cellular respiration mainly take place?
104127.e: Mitochondria are seen as the power stations of the cell. There, energy is obtained from nutrients using oxygen.
104127.m: The mitochondria are the power stations of the cell.

104128.q: Why do you breathe faster during physical exercise?
104128.e: Working muscles need a lot of energy, which they get through cellular respiration. This requires more oxygen, and more carbon dioxide has to be removed.
104128.m: During exercise we breathe faster because the muscles need more oxygen.

104129.q: When do plants carry out cellular respiration?
104129.e: Every living cell needs energy all the time. That is why plants always respire, even when they are carrying out photosynthesis at the same time during the day.

a: The cell gets energy from nutrients
104130.e: In cellular respiration, sugar is broken down with oxygen. The cell needs the energy released in order to live.
104130.m: Cellular respiration supplies the cell with energy.

104131.q: What is getting energy from sugar without oxygen called?
104131.e: Without oxygen, some cells can only break down sugar incompletely. This produces much less energy than cellular respiration.
104131.m: Fermentation supplies energy without oxygen, but only a little.

104132.q: Which substance forms in muscle cells when they get too little oxygen during hard exercise?
104132.e: When oxygen is short, muscle cells get energy through lactic acid fermentation. This produces lactic acid, or lactate.
104132.m: When oxygen is short, muscles produce lactic acid.

104133.q: Which process, in terms of its overall balance, runs roughly in reverse to photosynthesis?
104133.e: Photosynthesis builds up sugar from carbon dioxide and water and gives off oxygen. Cellular respiration breaks sugar down again with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water.
104133.m: In their overall balance, cellular respiration and photosynthesis are opposites.

104134.q: Why does a compost heap get warm inside?
a: Tiny organisms respire and give off heat
The sun heats it from below
104134.e: Bacteria and fungi break down the plant remains and respire as they do so. Some of the energy released is given off as heat.

104135.q: How does the carbon dioxide produced in cellular respiration leave the human body?
a: Through the lungs when you breathe out
104135.e: The blood carries carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs. There it is released into the air sacs and breathed out.
104135.m: We breathe out carbon dioxide through the lungs.

104136.q: What are the two bean-shaped cells around a stoma called?
104136.e: Two guard cells lie side by side like two beans, leaving a gap between them. The leaf exchanges gases with the air through this gap.
104136.m: Guard cells open and close the stoma.

104137.q: What happens to the guard cells when a stoma opens?
a: They take in water and curve
They lose water and go limp
104137.e: When the guard cells take in water, they swell and curve because their walls are unevenly thick. This creates a gap between them.
104137.m: Swollen guard cells open the stoma.

104139.q: What escapes through the stomata during transpiration?
104139.e: Water evaporates out of the leaf through the open stomata. This pull helps to draw water up from the roots.

104140.q: Why do many plants close their stomata in great heat and drought?
104140.e: Closed stomata stop too much water evaporating. In return, less carbon dioxide can get into the leaf.
104140.m: In drought, the plant closes its stomata.

104141.q: How many guard cells surround a stoma?
104141.e: Two bean-shaped guard cells lie side by side, leaving a gap between them. In technical language, such an opening is called a stoma.
104141.m: Two guard cells form a stoma.

104142.q: Which plants of dry regions open their stomata mainly at night to save water?
104142.e: Cacti take in carbon dioxide at night, when it is cooler, and store it as an acid. During the day the stomata stay closed and photosynthesis uses the store.
104142.m: Cacti open their stomata in the cool night.

104143.q: Which instrument can you use to look closely at the stomata of a thin layer of leaf skin?
104143.e: Stomata are only fractions of a millimetre in size. A light microscope magnifies them enough for you to make out the guard cells.
104143.m: You see stomata under the microscope.

104144.q: What does a green plant make from water and carbon dioxide during photosynthesis?
104144.e: Using the energy of sunlight, the plant builds up sugar from water and carbon dioxide. In this way, outside substances become the plant's own substances.
104144.m: Plants build up sugar with sunlight.

104145.q: Which living things can make their own food with the help of sunlight?
104145.e: Green plants use sunlight to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. That is why they are called autotrophs, or self-feeders.

104146.q: Why do humans and animals have to eat food?
a: They can't make nutrients from light
They have to exercise their teeth
104146.e: Humans, animals and fungi can't build nutrients from light and carbon dioxide. They take in ready-made nutrients with their food.
104146.m: Humans and animals depend on food.

104147.q: Which gas does a plant take in from the air during photosynthesis?
104147.e: The plant takes in carbon dioxide through its leaves. It builds the carbon into sugar and gives off oxygen.
104147.m: Plants take in carbon dioxide and give off oxygen.

104148.q: What is the process called in which cells break down sugar with oxygen to obtain energy?
104148.e: In cellular respiration, sugar is broken down with oxygen. This releases energy and produces carbon dioxide and water.
104148.m: Cellular respiration supplies cells with energy.

104149.q: Which plants can use nitrogen from the air thanks to nodule bacteria on their roots?
104149.e: Nodule bacteria turn nitrogen from the air into a form that plants can use. Clover, beans and peas live together with them.
104149.m: Clover and beans use nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria.

104150.q: Which living things make food at hot springs in the deep sea, even though no sunlight reaches there?
104150.e: Some bacteria get energy from chemical substances that flow out of hot springs. With it they build up food without light.
104150.m: Some bacteria make food without light.

104151.q: What does a plant take in from the soil through its roots together with water?
104151.e: Along with the water, the roots take in dissolved mineral salts, for example nitrogen salts. The plant uses them to build proteins, among other things.
104151.m: Plants get mineral salts from the soil.

104152.q: Which gas does a plant give off in total darkness?
104152.e: In the dark there is no photosynthesis, but cellular respiration continues. This gives off carbon dioxide.
104152.m: In the dark, plants give off carbon dioxide.
